leftCard.title: Forward Price (F_t)
leftCard.subtitle: New Agreement Delivery Price
points: Agreed transaction price for future delivery.
Set by market so that initial value equals zero (f = 0).
Changes daily as market expectations and spot prices shift.

rightCard.title: Contract Value (f)
rightCard.subtitle: Existing Position Mark-to-Market
points: The economic dollar worth of an existing contract today.
Starts at zero at inception (t = 0).
Can turn heavily positive or negative as spot moves away from strike K.

data.contrast: Delivery price for new contracts vs MTM value of existing commitments

semantics.teachingObjective: Contrast delivery price against mark-to-market contract value

beats.hindi_tts: The forward price is the delivery price that makes a brand new contract cost zero to enter. It recalibrates continuously as spot prices move.

beats.en_narration: The forward price is the delivery price that makes a brand new contract cost zero to enter. It recalibrates continuously as spot prices move.

leftCard.title: Forward Price (F_t)
leftCard.subtitle: New Agreement Delivery Price
points: Formula: F_t = S_t · e^(r·tau).
Requires zero initial cash transfer between counterparties.
Represents current cost of carry from today until maturity.

rightCard.title: Contract Value (f)
rightCard.subtitle: Existing Position Mark-to-Market
points: Formula: f = (F_t - K) · e^(-r·tau).
Measures the cash needed to close out or transfer the contract today.
Becomes positive if spot rises above delivery strike K.

data.contrast: F_t sets zero cost; f discounts the spread (F_t - K)

semantics.teachingObjective: Explain how F_t establishes parity and f measures divergence from locked strike

beats.hindi_tts: In contrast, contract value f represents the present value of the spread between the current forward price F_t and your locked strike K.
beats.en_subtitle: Contract value f is the present value of the spread between new forward price and strike K.
beats.en_narration: In contrast, contract value f represents the present value of the spread between the current forward price F_t and your locked strike K.

leftCard.title: Forward Price (F_t)
leftCard.subtitle: Benchmark Price
points: New forward price for 3 months: $53 · e^(0.06·0.25) = $53.80.
Zero value for anyone entering the trade today.
Pure benchmark for future settlement.

rightCard.title: Contract Value (f)
rightCard.subtitle: Raju's Locked Position
points: Spread: ($53.80 - $50.00) = $3.80 at maturity.
Discounted spread: $3.80 · e^(-0.015) = +$3.74 today.
Both formula paths yield the exact identical mark-to-market value!

data.contrast: f = (F_t - K) * e^(-r*tau) identical to S_t - K*e^(-r*tau)

semantics.teachingObjective: Prove mathematical equivalence of both forward valuation expressions

leftCard.title: Cash-and-Carry Arbitrage
leftCard.subtitle: When Futures Overvalued (F_market > F_0)
points: Borrow cash at risk-free rate r.
Buy the constituent basket of 500 spot stocks.
Sell index futures contracts simultaneously.
Collect stock dividends q and deliver basket at maturity.

rightCard.title: Reverse Cash-and-Carry
rightCard.subtitle: When Futures Undervalued (F_market < F_0)
points: Short sell the constituent basket of 500 spot stocks.
Invest the short sale proceeds at risk-free rate r.
Buy index futures contracts simultaneously.
Pay manufactured dividends and buy back basket at maturity.

data.contrast: Simultaneous basket trading across NYSE spot and CME futures

semantics.teachingObjective: Explain two-way index arbitrage mechanisms

beats.hindi_tts: If futures are overvalued, arbitrageurs borrow cash, buy the underlying five hundred stock basket, and sell futures, locking in riskless carry profit.
beats.en_subtitle: If futures trade rich, arbitrageurs borrow cash, buy the 500 stock basket, and sell futures, locking pure carry profit.
beats.en_narration: If futures are overvalued, arbitrageurs borrow cash, buy the underlying five hundred stock basket, and sell futures, locking in riskless carry profit.

leftCard.title: Program Trading Execution
leftCard.subtitle: Direct Computerized Routing
points: Computers monitor basis: Basis = Spot - Futures.
Instantly split orders across all 500 stock order books.
Locks in the riskless spread between futures and index basket.
Drives the futures price back down toward parity.

rightCard.title: Reverse Carry Execution
rightCard.subtitle: Institutional Shorting
points: Index fund managers swap physical stock holdings into cheap futures.
Invest proceeds in Treasury bills earning rate r.
Captures excess yield without adding market beta risk.
Drives the futures price back up toward parity.

data.contrast: Computer algorithms force futures and spot index into tight lockstep

semantics.teachingObjective: Detail program trading execution and market parity restoration

beats.hindi_tts: And if futures trade cheap, computers short the stock basket and buy futures within seconds. This automated workflow is called program trading.
beats.en_subtitle: If futures trade cheap, computers short the stock basket and buy futures in seconds via program trading.
beats.en_narration: And if futures trade cheap, computers short the stock basket and buy futures within seconds. This automated workflow is called program trading.

leftCard.title: Normal Market Efficiency
leftCard.subtitle: Tight Parity Bands
points: Arbitrage keeps futures within 0.1% to 0.2% of fair value.
Requires instantaneous order execution on both exchanges.
Assumes continuous liquidity in all constituent stocks.

rightCard.title: Execution Vulnerability
rightCard.subtitle: The Dependency on Order Flow
points: If exchange order routing queues delay stock trades, arbitrage breaks.
Cash index prices become stale if individual stocks halt trading.
Sets the stage for massive systemic crashes when liquidity evaporates.

data.contrast: Parity relies on instant two-way order execution without system latency

semantics.teachingObjective: Highlight reliance on order routing latency and introduce crisis vulnerabilities

cards.title: 1. The Black Monday Plunge
cards.subtitle: October 19, 1987 · Dow Drops 22.6%
cards.description: The Dow plummeted 508 points in a single session. Institutional portfolio insurance programs began dumping massive quantities of S&P 500 futures contracts automatically as spot prices fell.

cards.title: 2. The Futures Discount Chasm
cards.subtitle: Severe Unprecedented Backwardation
cards.description: Portfolio insurance selling overwhelmed CME floor market makers. S&P 500 futures traded at discounts of up to 40 index points below reported cash index levels.

cards.title: 3. NYSE DOT System Congestion
cards.subtitle: Order Transmission Delays > 2 Hours
cards.description: Arbitrageurs attempted to buy cheap futures and sell spot stocks, but the NYSE Designated Order Turnaround (DOT) system jammed with 100M+ unexecuted sell orders. Stock quotes became stale.

cards.title: 4. Regulatory Market Reforms
cards.subtitle: Circuit Breakers & Rule 80A
cards.description: Regulators instituted market-wide trading halts (circuit breakers) and NYSE Rule 80A collars to prevent runaway automated selling cascades during severe market dislocations.

leftCard.title: Contango (Normal Carry)
leftCard.subtitle: Futures Trade Above Spot (F_0 > S_0)
points: Total carry cost exceeds convenience yield (r + u > y).
Full supply and overflowing storage tanks.
Futures price curves slope upward over time.
Storage operators make steady returns buying spot and selling futures.

rightCard.title: Backwardation (Inverted Market)
rightCard.subtitle: Futures Trade Below Spot (F_0 < S_0)
points: Convenience yield exceeds carry cost (y > r + u).
Physical inventory is scarce; users demand immediate spot delivery.
Futures price curves slope downward over time.
Reverse cash-and-carry fails because refiners will not sell physical stock!

data.contrast: Upward sloping carry curve vs downward sloping convenience shortage curve

semantics.teachingObjective: Contrast contango and backwardation market structures

beats.hindi_tts: In contango, abundant inventory keeps futures prices above spot, compensating commercial storage operators for financing and warehousing.

beats.en_narration: In contango, abundant inventory keeps futures prices above spot, compensating commercial storage operators for financing and warehousing.

leftCard.title: Contango Economics
leftCard.subtitle: Full Carrying Charge Market
points: Arbitrage cap: F_0 cannot exceed S_0 · e^(r+u)T.
If futures trade higher, cash-and-carry buying spot floods storage.
Normal state for gold, silver, and well-supplied crude oil.
Negative roll yield for long futures holders.

rightCard.title: Backwardation Economics
rightCard.subtitle: Shortage Driven Supply Squeeze
points: No lower arbitrage bound exists for consumption commodities.
Manufacturers cannot lend or short scarce raw materials.
Generates positive roll yield for long futures investors.
Classic indicator of acute supply shocks and geopolitical risk.

data.contrast: Upper bound strictly enforced by arbitrage; lower bound unconstrained

leftCard.title: Contango Roll Yield
leftCard.subtitle: Headwind for Long Investors

Can produce massive drag on commodity ETF returns.
Seen during supertanker storage gluts.

rightCard.title: Backwardation Roll Yield
rightCard.subtitle: Tailwind for Long Investors

Provides substantial returns to long commodity positions.
Reflects the premium the market pays holders for releasing inventory.

scenes.title: The Whole Picture: 8 Core Forward Pricing Laws

beats.hindi_tts: The complete chapter at a glance: The eight fundamental laws of forward and futures pricing!

ui_state.heading: The 8 Core Forward Pricing Laws
steps: 1. Mid-Life Contract Value: Long forward value f = S_t - K·e^(-r·tau) discounts the delivery strike.
2. Contract Value vs Price: Forward price F_t enters at zero cost; contract value f tracks mark-to-market P&L.
3. Stock Index Futures: Continuous dividend yield q reduces carry: F_0 = S_0·e^((r - q)T).
4. Index Arbitrage: Program trading enforces cash-and-carry bounds across CME futures and NYSE baskets.
5. 1987 Crash Breakdown: Portfolio insurance cascades jammed NYSE DOT order printers, decoupling futures from spot.
6. Covered Interest Parity: Foreign interest rates act as continuous dividends: F_0 = S_0·e^((r - r_f)T).
7. Covered FX Arbitrage: Any forward currency divergence allows instant riskless borrowing and foreign conversion.
8. Convenience Yield Dynamics: In commodity shortages, high convenience yield y produces backwardation: F_0 < S_0.
ui_state.bottomTakeaway: Forward and futures prices reflect the net cost of carry across all asset classes.
